title: The 4 Properties of an اِسْم (Ism)
description: 20 questions on the Status, Number, Gender and Type of an اِسْم.
source: Owner’s lesson notes: three kinds of words and the 4 properties of an اِسْم

questions.text: An اِسْم has 4 properties. Which list names them correctly?
questions.explanation: The 4 properties of an اِسْم are Status, Number, Gender and Type. Tense belongs to the فِعْل (it is stuck in time), not to the اِسْم, which is timeless.

questions.text: What are the 3 statuses of an اِسْم?

options.text: Fully flexible, Partly flexible and Non-flexible

questions.explanation: Status has 3 forms: رَفْعَ for the doer, نَصْب for details, and جَرْ for the word after “of”. Singular/Dual/Plural is Number, and Common/Proper is Type.

questions.text: In “He drank juice outside yesterday quickly”, what is the status of “He”?

options.text: It is a فِعْل, not an اِسْم

questions.explanation: “He” is the doer of the action (drank), and the doer is in رَفْعَ status.

questions.text: In “The balloon of Abdallah popped loudly”, what is the status of “Abdallah”?

options.text: It is a حَرْف, not an اِسْم

questions.explanation: “Abdallah” comes right after “of” (the balloon of Abdallah), and the word after “of” is in جَرْ status.

questions.text: In Arabic, how do you tell which word is the doer (رَفْعَ) and which is a detail (نَصْب)?

options.text: By the order of the words in the sentence
By the sound at the end of each word
By whether the word starts with ال
By which word comes straight after the فِعْل

questions.explanation: In English the order of words tells you who did what, but in Arabic the order does not matter. The ending sound (or ending combination) of each word shows its status.

questions.text: A singular اِسْم ending in the sound “u” or “un” (as in مُسْلِمٌ) is in which status?
questions.explanation: For singular words, u/un means رَفْعَ, a/an means نَصْب, and i/in means جَرْ. مُسْلِمٌ ends in “un”, so it is رَفْعَ.

questions.text: What does the ending of مُسْلِمَانِ tell you?

options.text: Dual (a pair), in نَصْب or جَرْ status

questions.explanation: The ending “aani” marks a dual in رَفْعَ. A dual in نَصْب or جَرْ ends in “ayni”, as in مُسْلِمَيْنِ.

questions.text: What does the ending of مُسْلِمَاتٌ tell you?

options.text: Feminine plural, in نَصْب or جَرْ status

questions.explanation: “Aatun” is the feminine plural in رَفْعَ. With “aatin”, as in مُسْلِمَاتٍ, the word would be in نَصْب or جَرْ.

questions.text: What is the light version of مُسْلِمَانِ?
questions.explanation: مُسْلِمَانِ is heavy because of its ending combination. To make it light, remove the ن at the end: مُسْلِمَانِ becomes مُسْلِمَا.

questions.text: Which word is partly flexible (it can never take tanween or kasrah)?
questions.explanation: يُوسُفَ is a non-Arab name, so it is partly flexible: it never takes tanween or kasrah. مُسْلِمٌ and كِتَابٌ are fully flexible, and مُوسَى is non-flexible.

questions.text: How are non-human plurals (such as “books”) treated for gender and number?
questions.explanation: Plurals of things that aren’t human are treated as “she”: feminine and singular. “These are books” becomes “she is books”.

questions.text: أَقْلَامٌ (pens) is the plural of قَلَمٌ (pen). What kind of plural is it?

options.text: Human broken plural, treated as “she” or “they”
Non-human broken plural, treated only as “she”

questions.explanation: أَقْلَامٌ is a new word, not قَلَمٌ plus an ending combination, so it is a broken plural. Pens are not human, so the only choice is feminine singular (“she”).

questions.text: قَوْمٌ (a nation) looks singular. Why is it treated as plural?

options.text: It ends in a masculine plural combination
It is an Ism Jam’a (اسم جمع): plural by meaning, because the Arabs said so
It is a non-human feminine plural

questions.explanation: Words like قَوْمٌ (nation), نَاسٌ (people) and قَرْنٌ (generation) look singular but are plural by meaning (Ism Jam’a), because the Arabs said so.

questions.text: The masculine plural (ending “oona/eena”, as in مُسْلِمُونَ) is used only for…
questions.explanation: The masculine plural is used only for humans, angels and jinn, and it includes both males and females.

questions.text: What is the default gender of an اِسْم?
questions.explanation: Every اِسْم is masculine by default unless it falls into one of the feminine categories. Arabic has only “he” and “she”; there is no “it”.

questions.text: Which word is feminine because of its ending (a “fake feminine”)?
questions.explanation: آيَةً ends in ة, the most common sign of a fake feminine. خَوْفٌ, الجُوعِ and طَوْلًا are masculine singular.

questions.text: Which word is feminine because “the Arabs said so”?
questions.explanation: شَمْس has no feminine ending, but it is one of the words the Arabs treat as feminine, together with war, sky, fire, wind, land and the others in the story.

questions.text: What type is an اِسْم with tanween, such as كِتَابٌ?

options.text: Proper, because it names a thing

questions.explanation: Handy tip: if you see an اِسْم with tanween, it is common. Words with ال cannot have tanween, and names, pronouns and pointers are proper.

questions.text: Which word is proper?
questions.explanation: المُسْلِمُ has ال (“the”), one of the 7 categories of proper words. The other words have tanween, so they are common.

questions.text: What does the Ism Mowsool الَّذِينَ mean?
questions.explanation: الَّذِي means “the one who”, الَّذَانِ means “the two who”, and الَّذِينَ means “those who” (masculine plural).
